column3: Three preparations are examined. P has a cell wall, cytoplasmic ribosomes and division on a suitable cell-free nutrient medium. Q contains a nucleic-acid genome within a protein coat and multiplies only in host cells. R is a small circular infectious RNA without a protein coat. Which assignment is supported by all the observations?
column4: P virus; Q moneran; R viroid
column5: P moneran; Q virus; R viroid
column6: P moneran; Q viroid; R virus
column7: P viroid; Q virus; R moneran
column9:
Answer: (B) P moneran, Q virus and R viroid.
Why: P has cellular machinery and can divide without a living host, which distinguishes it from the acellular infectious preparations. A nucleic-acid genome enclosed by a protein coat is consistent with a virus in Q. The infectious naked circular RNA in R matches a viroid, whose organisation lacks a viral protein capsid. Host dependence alone would not distinguish Q from R; coat and cellular evidence must be used together.
Why not the others: (A) reverses the cellular and coated acellular preparations. (C) assigns a protein coat to a viroid and removes that defining distinction from the virus. (D) calls a dividing ribosome-containing cell a viroid and an acellular RNA a moneran.
Key point: Combine cellular organisation, independent division and the presence of a capsid when classifying an infectious preparation.
column10: Cellular division and capsid evidence separate a moneran, virus and viroid
column11: Biological classification: Kingdom Monera; Viruses and Viroids

column3: A flowering plant has alternate leaves and the illustrated bisexual, actinomorphic flower. Five stamens are attached to the united corolla. The two fused carpels form a superior ovary with axile placentation; fruit is a berry or capsule. Which family best matches the combined evidence?
column9:
Answer: (C) Solanaceae.
Why: The combination of a five-parted united calyx and corolla, five epipetalous stamens, and a bicarpellary superior ovary with axile placentation is characteristic of Solanaceae in the standard family description. The berry-or-capsule fruit supports that assignment. A single trait such as a superior ovary is shared by several families, so the linked whorl arrangement and ovule attachment are more informative than that trait alone.
Why not the others: (A) ordinarily has the distinctive papilionaceous organisation, ten stamens and a monocarpellary legume-producing gynoecium. (B) has a trimerous floral organisation and usually six stamens rather than the illustrated pentamerous one. (D) has the reduced grass-flower organisation rather than the stated five-petalled epipetalous flower.
Key point: Identify a family from a correlated suite of floral and fruit characters rather than one shared feature.
column10: A family assignment combines epipetalous stamens, carpel fusion and fruit type
column11: Morphology of flowering plants: Description of Some Important Families; Solanaceae

column3: An isolated lysosomal fraction contains a protein-digesting enzyme. An added large protein substrate cannot cross intact lysosomal membranes. Little digestion occurs with intact vesicles in pH 5 buffer; detergent disruption gives strong digestion at pH 5 but little at pH 7. Enzyme amount is unchanged. Which explanation fits both interventions?
column4: Membrane sequestration and an acidic activity optimum restrict where digestion occurs
column5: The enzyme is absent until detergent synthesises it
column6: The substrate is digested only when the lysosomal membrane pumps ATP into it
column7: Detergent raises protein concentration equally at both pH values, fully explaining the difference
column9:
Answer: (A) Compartmentalisation and acidic conditions restrict digestion.
Why: Before disruption, the externally added substrate is physically separated from the enzyme, even though the surrounding buffer has a favourable pH. Detergent removes that access barrier, revealing substantial activity at pH 5. The weak rate at pH 7 despite equal enzyme amount shows that access alone is insufficient; catalytic groups and structure also depend on an appropriate acidic environment. The two interventions therefore expose different constraints on the same preparation.
Why not the others: (B) contradicts the stated unchanged enzyme amount and gives detergent an unsupported synthetic role. (C) replaces enzyme-substrate access with an unstated ATP-driven mechanism. (D) cannot explain why the disrupted preparations differ when enzyme amount and substrate supply are controlled.
Key point: Separate compartment access from chemical conditions when interpreting an organelle-enzyme assay.
column10: A substrate-access intervention is distinguished from a lysosomal pH requirement
column11: Cell: the unit of life: Endomembrane System; Lysosomes

column3: In a stipulated respiratory preparation, one glucose completes glycolysis and both pyruvates are oxidised to acetyl-CoA, but acetyl-CoA cannot enter the Krebs cycle. NAD+ is regenerated by an external system that makes no ATP. Count only net substrate-level ATP and CO2 from those completed stages. What are the two yields per glucose?
column9:
Answer: (D) 2 ATP and 2 CO2.
Given: Glycolysis and two pyruvate-oxidation reactions finish; no Krebs turnover or external ATP formation occurs.
Formula/Principle: Add the stage-specific carbon and substrate-level ATP balances rather than the full aerobic yield.
Step 1: Glycolysis converts one six-carbon glucose into two three-carbon pyruvates, releases no CO2 and has net ATP yield \[4-2=2	ext{ ATP}.\]
Step 2: Each pyruvate loses one carbon as CO2 on conversion to a two-carbon acetyl group. Thus \[n(\ce{CO2})=2(1)=2	ext{ molecules per glucose}.\]
Step 3: Krebs-cycle ATP and CO2 are absent because its stated entry step is blocked.
Why: Producing acetyl-CoA is not the same as oxidising its two carbons through the cycle. External NAD+ regeneration allows the named earlier reactions to continue without silently adding oxidative-phosphorylation ATP. This is a defined stage-accounting model, not the total yield of an intact cell oxidising glucose completely.
Why not the others: (A) counts the two glycolytic ATP investments as retained ATP. (B) assigns all six glucose carbons to CO2 despite the retained acetyl groups. (C) assumes the downstream block stops completed upstream reactions even with the supplied cofactor regeneration.
Key point: Reconstruct ATP and carbon outputs only from stages that actually operate.
column10: Respiratory-stage accounting stops at acetyl-CoA despite cofactor recycling
column11: Respiration in plants: Glycolysis; Aerobic Respiration; Respiratory Balance Sheet

column3: In a simplified blood-antigen model, a recipient's red cells agglutinate with anti-A and anti-B test sera but not anti-D. The recipient already has anti-D antibodies after a previous sensitisation. Donors are D1=A Rh-negative, D2=O Rh-positive and D3=AB Rh-negative. Ignore all non-ABO/Rh antigens. Which packed-red-cell and plasma pairing avoids the stated antigen-antibody conflicts?
column4: D2 red cells and D3 plasma
column5: D3 red cells and D1 plasma
column6: D1 red cells and D3 plasma
column7: D1 red cells and D2 plasma
column9:
Answer: (C) D1 red cells with D3 plasma.
Why: Reaction with both ABO antisera identifies A and B antigens on the recipient's cells, while the negative anti-D test identifies absence of the D antigen. The pre-existing anti-D makes D-positive donor red cells incompatible in this stated model. D1's A-positive, D-negative red cells introduce neither an ABO antigen foreign to this AB recipient nor D. D3's AB plasma lacks the ordinary anti-A and anti-B antibodies that would otherwise attack the recipient's cells. Red-cell and plasma compatibility must be analysed in opposite directions because one supplies antigens and the other supplies antibodies.
Why not the others: (A) introduces D-positive cells into a recipient with anti-D. (B) supplies group-A plasma containing anti-B against the recipient's B-bearing cells. (D) supplies group-O plasma with anti-A and anti-B against the recipient's AB cells.
Key point: In an antigen-antibody model, analyse donor-cell antigens and donor-plasma antibodies separately; actual transfusion practice additionally requires clinical compatibility procedures.
column10: An antigen assay and sensitisation history constrain two different blood components
column11: Body fluids and circulation: Blood Groups; ABO and Rh Grouping

column3: In an idealised male reproductive preparation, both vasa deferentia are interrupted while testes, their blood supply and accessory glands remain functional. Which observation distinguishes this intervention from removal of the testes?
column4: Semen contains no sperm despite maintained testosterone and ongoing sperm formation within the testes
column5: No semen is produced because all seminal fluid originates in the testes
column6: Testosterone immediately disappears because it normally travels through the vas deferens
column7: The urethra cannot carry urine because the vas deferens is its only outlet
column9:
Answer: (A) Sperm transport is interrupted while testicular functions persist.
Why: The vas deferens carries sperm away from the testis-associated storage and transport pathway. Interrupting that route prevents sperm from reaching the ejaculate, but does not remove the tissue that produces sperm or the Leydig cells that release testosterone into blood. Accessory glands can still contribute seminal secretions. The observation therefore separates transport failure from loss of endocrine and gamete-producing organs.
Why not the others: (B) ignores accessory-gland contributions to seminal fluid. (C) assigns a blood-borne hormone to the sperm duct as its necessary transport route. (D) confuses the reproductive duct connection with the separate bladder-to-urethra urinary route.
Key point: A blocked reproductive transport route need not abolish gamete formation or endocrine secretion.
column10: A reproductive-duct intervention separates transport, gametogenesis and endocrine function
column11: Human reproduction: Male Reproductive System; Reproductive health: Birth Control

column3: Two candidate donors have identical profiles at every VNTR locus assayed in a DNA-fingerprinting experiment. A trace sample matches that shared profile. With no other identifying evidence, which conclusion is justified?
column4: The trace must contain equal DNA amounts from both candidates
column5: The trace is compatible with either candidate, so these assayed markers do not identify which one contributed it
column6: The candidates must differ at every untested genomic position
column7: Matching profiles prove that no mutation ever occurred in either candidate
column9:
Answer: (B) Either candidate is compatible with the assayed profile.
Why: A profile is a set of observations at selected variable loci. When both candidates share those observations, matching the trace does not distinguish them within the assay's information. It also does not demonstrate that both contributed DNA, because one donor alone could produce the same result. Broader identity or mutation-history claims require evidence beyond the markers actually measured.
Why not the others: (A) turns compatibility with two sources into proof of a two-source mixture and an unmeasured mixture ratio. (C) infers universal difference at unobserved positions from equality at the observed ones. (D) makes an absolute historical claim that a finite marker panel cannot establish.
Key point: State what a fingerprint can distinguish in the candidate set, not what its name suggests it should identify.
column10: Identical assayed VNTR profiles limit individual identification without implying a mixture
column11: Molecular basis of inheritance: DNA Fingerprinting

column3: Three transmission models are considered: malaria, filariasis and typhoid. An intervention prevents mosquito bites but does not change drinking-water contamination, sanitation or existing infections. Which pair is expected to have reduced new vector-mediated transmission, and why?
column4: Malaria and typhoid, because both multiply in mosquito salivary glands
column5: Filariasis and typhoid, because both require mosquito entry into the intestine
column6: Typhoid alone, because all mosquito-borne infections are bacterial
column7: Malaria and filariasis, because both include a mosquito-mediated entry route
column9:
Answer: (D) Malaria and filariasis.
Why: Malaria and filarial infection are transmitted through mosquito vectors in the standard disease cycles, even though their causative organisms and vector associations differ. Blocking bites interrupts that shared exposure route without directly killing pathogens already inside a host. Typhoid is associated with ingestion of contaminated food or water rather than a required mosquito-bite stage, so the stipulated intervention does not directly remove its route. This prediction concerns new transmission, not an immediate cure or a measured effect size.
Why not the others: (A) wrongly inserts typhoid into a mosquito cycle. (B) again makes typhoid vector-borne and misplaces the mosquito's role. (C) misclassifies the protozoan and helminth infections as bacteria and reverses the route-based prediction.
Key point: Compare the specific life-cycle entry route when predicting an intervention's direct effect.
column10: A vector-exposure control distinguishes protozoan and helminth routes from typhoid ingestion
column11: Human health and disease: Common Diseases in Humans; Malaria; Filariasis; Typhoid

column3: A recombinant bacterium makes a human proinsulin-like precursor but does not remove its connecting C peptide. Separately produced mature A and B chains can be joined with the correct disulfide bonds to give active insulin. Which interpretation best connects the results?
column4: A peptide bond joining the mature A and B chains is the missing permanent insulin linkage
column5: Bacteria cannot translate any human-derived amino-acid sequence
column6: Precursor processing and correct chain assembly are distinct requirements beyond making the initial polypeptide
column7: The C peptide must remain in every mature insulin molecule for receptor binding
column9:
Answer: (C) Processing and correct assembly matter beyond translation.
Why: Proinsulin contains a connecting segment that is removed during maturation. Mature insulin retains A and B chains linked by the appropriate disulfide arrangement rather than by retaining that C-peptide connector. Producing the precursor therefore does not guarantee producing the mature active molecule. Activity after correct assembly of separately produced chains shows that expression of human-derived chains is possible, while processing and folding remain separate biochemical tasks.
Why not the others: (A) substitutes a permanent interchain peptide connection for the stated mature disulfide linkage. (B) contradicts production and successful use of the recombinant chains. (D) reverses the role of the connecting peptide during normal maturation.
Key point: Distinguish expression, precursor processing and final protein assembly in a recombinant product.
column10: Proinsulin processing distinguished from expression and disulfide assembly of mature insulin
column11: Biotechnology and its application: Biotechnological Applications in Medicine; Insulin

column3: A two-age expected-population model starts with 40 juveniles and 80 adults. During each interval, half the initial juveniles survive and become adults; three-quarters of initial adults survive; each initial adult produces b new juveniles that are all present at the next census. In interval 1, 10 adults immigrate and 10 adults emigrate after reproduction. The next census totals 200. With the same b and survival rates but no migration in interval 2, what are b and the expected total at its end?
column9:
Answer: (B) b=1.50 and expected total 240.
Given: Only adults present at an interval's start reproduce; survival and maturation precede the next age census.
Formula/Principle: Keep births, surviving cohorts and migration separate before updating the age structure.
Step 1: Adults at census 1 are \[A_1=0.5(40)+0.75(80)+10-10=80.\]
Step 2: New juveniles are \(J_1=80b\), so \[80+80b=200\Rightarrow b=1.50,\quad J_1=120.\]
Step 3: For the second interval, \[J_2=1.5(80)=120,\quad A_2=0.5(120)+0.75(80)=120.\]
Step 4: \[N_2=J_2+A_2=240.\]
Why: The total count alone is insufficient for the next projection because juveniles and adults have different roles and survival. Births in one interval enlarge the next juvenile cohort but do not become same-interval breeders. Cancelling net migration does not justify omitting maturation or adult mortality. These are stipulated expected counts, not an assumption of logistic growth or a field estimate of carrying capacity.
Why not the others: (A) omits the 20 maturing juveniles when inferring b. (C) uses the 120 juveniles as if they were the current breeding adults in interval 2. (D) neither reproduces the observed census with the stated surviving adults nor updates its age composition.
Key point: Preserve cohort identity when moving from a population balance to a second projection.
column10: An observed census identifies reproduction before an age-structured second interval
column11: Organisms and populations: Populations; Natality; Mortality; Age Structure

column3: Island birds trace to one ancestral lineage but have diversified into several beak forms associated with different foods. In a separate comparison, distantly related mammalian lineages independently evolve similar burrowing body forms. Which interpretation uses ancestry as well as function?
column4: The birds illustrate adaptive radiation; the similar burrowing forms illustrate convergence
column5: The birds illustrate convergence because all eat; the mammals illustrate one shared recent radiation
column6: Both observations prove that useful forms arise by directed mutation in each individual
column7: Both comparisons demonstrate identical ancestry because ecological functions match
column9:
Answer: (A) Adaptive radiation in the birds and convergence in the mammalian comparison.
Why: Diversification from one ancestral stock into different ecological roles is the defining pattern of adaptive radiation. Similar adaptive forms appearing independently in distant lineages instead support convergent evolution. Functional similarity alone cannot establish a recent common origin, and different functions can arise among close relatives. The supplied ancestry observations therefore determine how the morphological similarities and differences are interpreted.
Why not the others: (B) discards the one-lineage origin of the birds and invents a shared recent origin for the distant mammals. (C) makes an unsupported claim about directed within-individual mutation rather than population evolution. (D) equates matching function with identical ancestry.
Key point: Use the ancestry pattern to distinguish divergence into niches from independent resemblance.
column10: Common ancestry with ecological divergence contrasted with independent functional resemblance
column11: Evolution: Adaptive Radiation; Evidence for Evolution; Convergent Evolution

column3: A respiratory-volume model has tidal volume 500 mL, inspiratory reserve 2000 mL, expiratory reserve 1000 mL and residual volume 1200 mL. What maximum volume can be expired after a maximal inspiration, without including air that remains after maximal expiration?
column9:
Answer: (C) 3500 mL.
Given: TV=500 mL, IRV=2000 mL, ERV=1000 mL and RV=1200 mL.
Formula/Principle: Vital capacity is the volume between maximal inspiration and maximal expiration.
Step 1: \[VC=IRV+TV+ERV.\]
Step 2: \[VC=2000+500+1000=3500	ext{ mL}.\]
Why: Residual volume stays in the lungs after the specified maximal expiration and is outside the requested moving volume. It contributes to total lung capacity, not to vital capacity. The calculation identifies the two endpoint states before combining the named volumes.
Why not the others: (A) includes residual volume and gives total lung capacity. (B) leaves out ordinary tidal volume. (D) adds residual volume to tidal volume while ignoring both reserves.
Key point: Define the starting and ending respiratory states before adding volume components.
column10: Vital capacity excludes the residual compartment despite a maximal inspiration
column11: Breathing and exchange of gases: Respiratory Volumes and Capacities

column3: Two hormone signals both promote mobilisation of glucose reserves. P is released rapidly from the adrenal medulla during acute stress. Q is a peptide released from pancreatic islets during fasting. Which assignment is correct?
column4: P cortisol; Q insulin from beta cells
column5: P adrenaline; Q insulin from alpha cells
column6: P thyroxine; Q glucagon from beta cells
column7: P adrenaline; Q glucagon from alpha cells
column9:
Answer: (D) Adrenaline and alpha-cell glucagon.
Why: The adrenal medulla supplies catecholamines such as adrenaline in the acute stress response. Pancreatic alpha cells release glucagon, which helps raise available glucose during fasting, whereas beta-cell insulin generally promotes glucose uptake and storage. Similar effects on a measured glucose variable do not make the hormones identical or give them the same tissue source. Source, cell type and physiological trigger jointly identify the pair.
Why not the others: (A) assigns the medullary rapid signal to a cortical hormone and pairs fasting mobilisation with insulin. (B) retains adrenaline but gives insulin the wrong islet cell and action. (C) substitutes thyroid hormone for the medullary signal and places glucagon in beta cells.
Key point: Combine endocrine source, trigger and action rather than identifying a hormone from one endpoint alone.
column10: An acute medullary signal and a fasting islet signal share an endpoint but not a source
column11: Chemical coordination and integration: Adrenal Gland; Pancreas; Hormone Action

column3: A plant cell has completed nuclear division. The figure shows Golgi-derived vesicles gathering between the two nuclei. A treatment now prevents those vesicles from fusing, but leaves the completed chromosome segregation intact. Which immediate outcome is most directly predicted?
column4: Two anucleate cells arise by a cleavage furrow
column5: The one cell retains two daughter nuclei and fails to build the initial cell plate
column6: The two nuclei fuse automatically into a haploid nucleus
column7: DNA replication must reverse before cytokinesis can begin
column9:
Answer: (B) A binucleate cell without the initial cell plate.
Why: In the depicted plant-cell cytokinesis route, vesicles fuse centrally to form the cell plate and associated new partition. Blocking their fusion prevents this cytoplasmic separation even though karyokinesis has already produced two daughter nuclei. No reversal of chromosome segregation is required for the cell to remain binucleate. The observed vesicle location identifies the relevant plant mechanism rather than an animal-type constricting furrow.
Why not the others: (A) substitutes a different cytokinesis mechanism and removes nuclei that the stem says are present. (C) invents nuclear fusion and a ploidy reduction with no stated cause. (D) assigns a backward DNA-synthesis requirement to a membrane-partitioning step.
Key point: Nuclear division and cytoplasmic partitioning are separable events with different cellular machinery.
column10: Vesicle-fusion blockade interrupts plant cytokinesis after successful nuclear separation
column11: Cell cycle and cell division: Mitosis; Cytokinesis in Plant Cells

column3: In a simplified early mammalian-development experiment, preparation X forms a blastocyst with functional trophoblast but loses its inner cell mass before attachment. Preparation Y retains an inner cell mass but its trophoblast cannot adhere to the endometrium. Other required conditions are maintained. Which paired prediction best separates the two lineage roles?
column4: X may attach and still form a normal embryo proper; Y implants because trophoblast adhesion is unnecessary after blastocyst formation
column5: X cannot attach solely because its inner cell mass is absent; Y's inner cell mass replaces the trophoblast and restores implantation
column6: Neither preparation can have reached a blastocyst because either lineage defect necessarily prevents the earlier cleavage divisions
column7: X may begin attachment but cannot form a normal embryo proper; Y can form a blastocyst but cannot implant by the specified route
column9:
Answer: (D) X separates attachment capacity from embryo formation; Y separates blastocyst formation from implantation.
Why: The trophoblast participates in attachment to the uterine lining and later maternal-fetal interactions, while the inner cell mass supplies the embryo proper. Losing the inner cell mass therefore does not logically erase an already formed trophoblast's initial adhesion capability, but it prevents normal embryo-proper development. Conversely, having an inner cell mass does not substitute for the specified trophoblast adhesion function. The stage chronology also matters: fertilisation and cleavage precede blastocyst attachment, so an implantation defect does not prove those earlier events never occurred. This deliberately limited model does not assert that a trophoblast alone forms every tissue of a complete placenta.
Why not the others: (A) ignores loss of the embryo-forming lineage and the specified adhesion defect. (B) confuses the attachment role of trophoblast with the embryo-proper role of inner cell mass. (C) infers failure of an earlier completed stage from a later functional defect.
Key point: Distinguish stage chronology from lineage-specific functions.
column10: Complementary blastocyst-lineage defects separate fertilisation, implantation and embryo-proper development
column11: Human reproduction: Fertilisation and Implantation; Pregnancy and Embryonic Development
